question: What is the purpose of acceptance criteria?
options: To decide which sprint a user story belongs in
To define how we know a user story has been completed correctly
To record who is responsible for writing the user story
To estimate how many story points a user story is worth

question: In the registration example (Bob wants to register so he can save videos), which of these is an acceptance criterion?
options: The story is worth five story points
A confirmation email should be sent to the user
As Bob, I want to register for an account so I can save videos for later viewing
The sprint goal is to launch the video library

question: Which is the correct order of the Gherkin keywords for acceptance criteria?
options: Given, When, Then (with And to add extra information)
Given, Then, When (with And to add extra information)
When, Given, Then (with And to add extra information)
Then, Given, When (with And to add extra information)

question: In Gherkin, what does each keyword mean?
options: Given is the action, When is the starting context, Then is the expected outcome
Given is the expected outcome, When is the starting context, Then is the action
Given is the starting context, When is the action, Then is the expected outcome
Given is the action, When is the expected outcome, Then is the starting context

question: The Given / When / Then format is used to structure which of these?
options: Epics, to group related stories together
Definitions of done, to confirm each story is complete
Acceptance criteria
User stories, to describe who wants what and why

question: 'Given I am on the sign-in screen and enter a valid email and a valid password, when I click Sign In, then I should see a welcome message and have access to my profile.' What kind of path is this?
options: An alternative path
The happy path
An unhappy alternative path
The sad path

question: 'Given I am on the sign-in page and enter a valid email and an invalid password, when I click Sign In, then I get an error message saying my credentials are incorrect.' What kind of path is this?
options: The sad path
The happy alternative path
The happy path
An alternative path

question: 'Given I have linked my account to a Facebook account, when I sign in via Facebook, then I should see a welcome message and have access to my profile.' What kind of path is this?
options: The sad path, because the user needs a different account
The main happy path, with nothing different from valid credentials
An alternative path, a happy alternative as the user still gets in
A non-functional requirement about security and compliance

question: Which three kinds of path may acceptance criteria need to cover?
options: Happy, sad and neutral, covering every user outcome
Main, backup and error, covering every user outcome
Happy, sad (unhappy) and alternative
Success, failure and retry, covering every user outcome

question: A customer on a T-shirt page selects a size that is out of stock. How is this best described, and how might it be avoided?
options: A non-functional requirement; it can only be fixed by scaling the system to handle more load
The happy path; nothing can be done to avoid it, because stock levels cannot be shown to users
An alternative path; the size filter should always be removed so the customer is not confused
A sad path; clever UX, such as greying out or labelling out-of-stock sizes, can prevent it

question: A group wrote 'Given I'm on the dashboard, when I click the status tab, then view wind speed, view temperature and view precipitation.' What improvement was suggested?
options: Remove the Given and keep only the When, since the user's location does not matter
Add more story points to the story, so that the extra detail is allowed for in the estimate
Be more specific about where the user is and what they should see, such as format, units and direction
Move the criteria into the definition of done, so that the developers can tick them off

question: Can one user story have more than one set of acceptance criteria?
options: Yes, different scenarios or paths may each need their own acceptance criteria
No, there is exactly one set of criteria for each story, whatever the paths
Yes, but only for the sad paths, because the happy path never needs criteria
No, acceptance criteria belong to epics, not to the user stories under them

question: Which description of the product backlog is correct?
options: A list owned by the development team that the product owner is not allowed to change
The list of items chosen for the current sprint, which the team works through in priority order
An ordered list of everything needed in the product and the single source of requirements; it is never complete
A fixed list of requirements agreed at the start of the project and finalised after the first sprint

question: Which information helps the product owner prioritise user stories?
options: Business value, estimated effort and dependencies
The number of stakeholders who attend the sprint review
The sprint length and the number of ceremonies
The Scrum Master's availability and the retrospective mood

question: In what can the estimated effort of a user story be represented?
options: The product owner's rating out of ten
The number of meetings needed
Lines of code
Time, or story points

question: What does planning poker estimate?
options: The business value of a user story
The length of the next sprint
The number of developers needed on the team
The effort a user story is likely to need

question: Which sequence correctly describes planning poker?
options: Discuss the story, the product owner reveals a card first, then everyone else matches that card
Everyone reveals a card in turn, the average is taken, and then the vote is final
Discuss the story, everyone picks a card, all reveal together, outliers explain, then vote again
Everyone picks a card, outliers explain their reasoning, all reveal together, then discuss the story

question: Why must everyone reveal their estimate at the same time in planning poker?
options: So that each person gives their own opinion rather than copying others
So that the Scrum Master can mark the quickest estimator
So that estimates can be used straight in the burn down chart
So that the product owner can approve the estimates faster

question: In planning poker, one person holds a 2 and another a 5. What happens?
options: The team tries to understand the reasoning behind the outliers, then estimates again
The two numbers are averaged and the result is used as the estimate for the story
The highest number is used to be safe, since it is better to over-estimate than under
The product owner picks which number is correct and the team moves on to the next story

question: What did the building-height estimation exercise demonstrate?
options: Explaining the reasoning behind outlying estimates helps the team converge on a more agreed estimate
The first estimate given is always the most accurate, so the rest of the team should follow it
Estimates should be given in whatever units each person prefers, to keep the range of opinion wide
The product owner should have the final say on estimates, as they know the business best

question: What does a burn down chart show?
options: The mood of the team across the sprint, with a point plotted for each day of the sprint
The story points completed, starting at zero and rising each day as the stories are done
The number of bugs found in each sprint, shown against the number that have since been fixed
The story points remaining in the sprint, starting at the total planned and falling as stories are done

question: A sprint burn down chart starts at 40. What does this mean?
options: The sprint is 40 days long and so has 40 daily scrums
The team has planned 40 story points of work for the sprint
The team has chosen 40 user stories for the sprint backlog
The product backlog contains 40 user stories to be done

question: What was the dashed line on the burn down chart most likely showing?
options: A guide to the points that should be remaining each day to stay on track
The date of the sprint review, which the team is working towards
The points that the stakeholders added to the sprint part-way through
The number of blockers that the team raised at each daily scrum

question: What do the letters in MoSCoW stand for?
options: Must have, Should have, Could have, Would have
Must have, Should have, Can have, Won't have
Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have
Must have, Shall have, Could have, Won't have

question: Which technique is used to prioritise requirements?
options: MoSCoW
Planning poker
Gherkin
A burn down chart

question: What is a minimum viable product (MVP)?
options: A version of a new product that lets the team gather maximum validated learning from customers with least effort
A wireframe that is shown to stakeholders before any development has started on the product
The final, complete version of the product, with every item on the backlog done and signed off
The goal of the first sprint, chosen by the product owner whatever the product needs to do

question: A team releases only the absolute essentials so users can start trying things and giving feedback. Which concept is this?
options: A definition of done
A minimum viable product
A sprint retrospective
A burn down chart

question: The story points for a sprint add up to 512, but the team can only handle 40. What does this show?
options: The burn down chart should start at 512 so that it shows the full amount of planned work
The team has a very ambitious but acceptable sprint goal that it can reach with extra effort
The team has taken on far too much, and the sprint is not ready to start
The product owner should add more stories, because the team has plenty of capacity left

question: What is the difference between a definition of ready and a definition of done?
options: Done is a checklist of prerequisites before starting; ready is a checklist confirming something has been completed properly
Both are checked after the work is finished, but by different roles
Ready is a checklist of prerequisites before starting; done is a checklist confirming something has been completed properly
Both are checked before the work starts, but at different levels

question: At which levels can a definition of ready and a definition of done apply?
options: Only the user story, because a sprint is too short to have one
Only the sprint, because the project is too large to have one
The project, the sprint and the user story
Only the project, because stories and sprints are covered by it

question: How does the checklist apply within a level, and between levels?
options: It is the same checklist for every item at that level, but different from the checklists at other levels
It is the same checklist for sprints and for user stories, and it applies to the whole project
It is set by Scrum and cannot be changed by the team, whatever the project or the product
It is different for every sprint and every user story, and is rewritten before each one begins

question: Who decides what goes into a team's definition of ready or done?
options: The stakeholders alone, who set the list when the contract for the project is written
The team decides its own checklist; the examples in the training are not fixed rules
Scrum fixes the list for every team, so that every project is measured in the same way
The Scrum Master alone, who then asks the team to sign it off at the retrospective

question: Which of these is an example of a definition of ready at the sprint level?
options: The documentation has been updated
The sprint goal has been agreed
The performance test has passed
The unit tests have passed on the code

question: The sprint backlog does not completely define what needs to be done in the sprint. What does this mean for the definition of ready?
options: The product owner must cancel the sprint and the stories go back into the product backlog
The team is not ready to start the sprint until those user stories are fleshed out
The team can start and flesh the stories out at the sprint review, once the stakeholders attend
The stories are moved straight to done, because the team will have enough detail later

question: Halfway through a sprint, the team finds that it does not have a subscription it needs. Which item was missing from its sprint-level definition of ready?
options: Test coverage has been checked
Necessary technical resources are available
Every user story is done
The bugs have been closed or postponed

question: Which sprint-level definition of ready item catches the problem of a story having to be done before another one?
options: Documentation has been updated
The acceptance tests have passed
Any dependencies have been resolved
The product owner and stakeholders are happy

question: Which of these is NOT part of a user-story definition of ready?
options: Any dependencies and blockers have been identified in advance
The acceptance criteria are written and agreed by the team
The code and unit tests have been checked into version control
The size of the story has been estimated by the team

question: Which of these is an example of a sprint-level definition of done?
options: Every user story on the sprint backlog is done and the performance test has passed
The sprint goal has been agreed and the technical resources are available
The user stories are estimated and prioritised, ready for sprint planning
The Three Amigos have met to discuss the story and agreed what it means

question: Why might a sprint-level definition of done include a performance test?
options: So the team does not find out later that the working software is very slow, a non-functional requirement
So the Scrum Master can check how quickly each developer is working during the sprint
So the burn down chart ends on zero and the sprint can be shown to have been a success
So the product owner can estimate the story points for the stories in the next sprint

question: Which of these also appears in an example sprint-level definition of done?
options: Enough time exists to complete the user stories in the sprint backlog, given the story points
The sprint backlog has been agreed and its stories are ready to be worked on in the sprint
The sprint goal has been agreed by the product owner and the whole of the development team
Bugs have been closed or postponed, and documentation has been updated

question: What does test coverage measure?
options: How many stakeholders have reviewed the increment
How much of the code is covered by tests, such as unit tests
How many requirements have acceptance criteria
How many sprints have been completed

question: What is a unit test?
options: A test where stakeholders try the full system and sign it off
A test that checks the Given / When / Then wording of the acceptance criteria
The most basic test, checking each part of the code and the different paths through it
A test of how the system performs under heavy load

question: Which of these belongs in a user-story definition of done?
options: The code and unit tests are in version control, the tests pass, the acceptance criteria are met and coding standards pass
The sprint goal is agreed, the sprint backlog is agreed and the technical resources are available
The user story is estimated, its dependencies are identified and its acceptance criteria are written
Every user story is done and the product owner has re-ordered the product backlog for the next sprint

question: What are linters used for in a definition of done?
options: To check that the code meets a certain coding standard
To estimate the story points for the code before it is written
To run the performance test on the code in each sprint
To deploy the code to production once the tests have passed

question: Acceptance criteria appear in two checklists at user-story level. Which statement is correct?
options: Both statements appear only in the definition of done, because both are checked as the story is completed
Neither statement appears in a checklist, because acceptance criteria are not part of ready or done
'Acceptance criteria are met' is in the definition of ready; 'acceptance criteria are written' is in the definition of done
'Acceptance criteria are written' is in the definition of ready; 'acceptance criteria are met' is in the definition of done

question: A developer's code for a story works, but it is not in version control and has no unit tests. Is the story done?
options: Yes, because it works and the sprint is nearly over
Yes, as long as the product owner is happy at the review
No, but only because the Scrum Master has not yet approved it
No, it does not yet meet the definition of done for a user story

question: What is a wireframe?
options: A list of the acceptance criteria for the app, written in the Given, When, Then structure
A finished, coloured design of the app, ready for the developers to copy into code line for line
A blueprint or skeleton of an app or website, usually without colour or fonts, showing navigation and options
A diagram of the database tables behind the app, showing how the data is stored and linked

question: How does a storyboard relate to a wireframe?
options: It is a list of all the user stories in the product backlog, ordered by business value
It is the final colour scheme and font selection, agreed with the stakeholders before coding
It is the test plan for the finished app, listing each test to be run before release
It shows the journey a user takes from screen to screen, often with a short description under each wireframe

question: Why is it useful to present wireframes to stakeholders early in the software development life cycle?
options: It means the requirements can be locked once the stakeholders have seen it, and never changed again
It removes the need for acceptance criteria, because the wireframe already shows what the user does
You get the maximum feedback as early as possible, and stakeholders often realise what they want when they see it
It means the product owner no longer needs to attend the sprint review at the end of the sprint

question: A stakeholder looks at a wireframe showing wind speed for the last three hours and asks whether it helps them decide about a jump tomorrow. What does this illustrate?
options: Stakeholders must not give feedback before development starts, since it slows the sprint down
The wireframe has failed its definition of done, so it must be redrawn before the stakeholder sees it
Stakeholders raise new needs when they see a visual, which fits welcoming changing requirements
The user story should never have been written, because it did not mention the forecast
